How to choose a therapist in Ventura County

Start with the practical filters: whether they take your insurance, whether they see people in person in Ventura County or by video, and whether they work with what you are bringing. Then read two or three profiles the way you would read a person, not a resume. The one whose words sound like someone you could talk to is usually the right first call.

Most therapists offer a short phone consultation before a first session. Use it to ask how they work, what a session costs, and how soon they can see you. Our guide to finding a therapist walks through the license letters, the costs and the questions worth asking.

What verified means here

A therapist cannot mark themselves verified. Each license is checked against the state board's own record, and the listing only goes public once that check is written down. A therapist's real phone number and email never appear on the site; you reach them through a Theraglee number and a contact form, so your first message goes to a practice that is what it says it is.

If you would rather be found

A free account includes Theraglee Match Mode: switch it on, pick the topics you want help with, and licensed therapists can reach out to you instead. You stay pseudonymous until you reply. Create a free account to turn it on.

Common questions

How much does therapy cost in Ventura County?

Roughly 100 to 250 dollars a session out of pocket in most of the country, more in expensive metros. In-network insurance reduces it to a copay, out-of-network plans often reimburse part of it, and many therapists keep a few sliding-scale slots that are not advertised. Ask on the consultation call.

Can I see a therapist in another state by video?

Usually not. A therapist has to be licensed in the state where you are sitting during the session, so a video therapist for someone in Ventura County needs a California license. Every listing shows the states the therapist is licensed in.

Does Theraglee recommend a therapist for me?

No. Theraglee is a directory and a set of self-help tools. It does not diagnose or treat anything, and it does not rank or recommend one therapist over another. Whether a therapist is right for you is your call and theirs.

What if I need help right now?

In the US you can call or text 988 at any time to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. A directory is for finding ongoing care, not for an emergency.
